paragraphs.text: Welcome back to another week of Tis the Podcast. The podcast that is determined to keep the spirit of Christmas alive 365 days a year. I'm Thom. I'm Julia. I'm Anthony.
How's everyone doing tonight?
Doing good. Good. So do you remember how I told you guys I did that painting thing at work into the Christmas tree?
This is it. A little tea latte.
Oh, look, it's cute.
That's fun. Good work, good work.
Thank you. And I also just wanted to show off something somebody got me: this "Don't Stop Believing" Santa, for my birthday.
They know you, don't they? They really know you.
It's so nice.
Yep. Can't beat a nice Christmas present for your birthday.
Not at all. That's part of having a birthday in a Brrr month.
There you go. Speaking of Brrr months, it's actually been brrr a bit here lately. Pretty excited.
I know. It actually feels like fall. I wore my podcast hoodie today.
Yay!
And still flip-flops.
Ridiculous.
No, I think my last pair of flip-flops broke yesterday while I was hauling in a 36-piece Christmas village that we bought at an estate sale.
Ooh, that sounds delightful. We bought a big Fontanini nativity set.
Oh, man. That sounds fancy. I know. We're all Christmas ready at the house. It looks kind of like we're moving because we have all this stuff in boxes right now.

So it's been cooling down here too, which is perfect, because I just took my car to get inspected for the year, and ever since I got it back, the air conditioning hasn't been working. And I was like, oh, that's totally fine. I'll forget all about it for a few months, and then the first hot day will hit, and I'll be like, oh no, my air.
Julia, are you still working downtown?
I am. I think we're on an egg timer at this point, but yeah, I am.
Go to Magic City and get a pumpkin spice mocha. It's amazing.
Is it? Is it not too sweet? Because I don't love sweet coffee drinks.
Oh, it's less sweet than anything you'd get at Starbucks. Even the plain coffee.
Perfect. I'm excited.
Have you guys been to Hallmark?
No, not yet.
Well, they have this Star Wars wreath. Have you seen it?
No.
It's like a black wreath that lights up, and you buy all the Star Wars ornaments individually, and they interact with each other and basically tell the story of the original trilogy.
That's really cool.
Yeah. So my mother got me the whole thing in one go for my birthday.
Good job, Mom.
Did y'all see the new La Crusade that's all Star Wars themed?
They have a baking oven that the top of it is Han Solo stuck in the carbonite.
That's awesome.
I saw one of those inflatable costumes for Halloween this year. Looks pretty funny.
Okay, this stuff is super cool. That Dutch oven that looks like R2-D2? Yes, please.
Okay, that's awesome.
I love that they're exhibiting a sense of humor, right? It's pretty fun. They're not just a fruity French brand. Best Dutch oven you can own.
I love it. It's awesome.
Oh, speaking of awesome: tonight we are covering the 1990 Tim Burton film Edward Scissorhands. Before we jump in, I'm assuming everybody has a long history with this movie, correct?
Yes.
Yep.
Do you want to start with your history, Julia?

Yeah. Shoot, when did I see this? I didn't see it in the movie theaters, because I probably wasn't allowed to, but I remember as soon as we could rent it, my brother brought it home, and it fascinated and freaked me out at the same time. And I've always had kind of a special place in my heart for this movie. Rewatching it this much later in life, because I hadn't seen this movie in years and years, there's a bunch of stuff I didn't notice watching it as a kid. So it was neat watching it again. It was still magical to me, and I still really enjoy this movie. What about you, Anthony?
I saw this movie for the first time a week ago, when we were supposed to record the episode.
That was the first time you'd seen it?
The first time I've seen this film. I remember as a kid just being freaked out by the look of Edward Scissorhands.
Why?

Why? I wonder why and yes I saw it for our first time a week ago when you're originally supposed to record this episode and I hated it That's the second time you've mentioned that we were supposed to record this last week we get it Did you say you hated this movie? I understand it's an unpopular opinion, but I hated this movie.
It's not like I don't see anything redeeming about it.
Spoiler alert: this is not going to be the only unpopular opinion I have in our Brrr Month episodes, so stay tuned for that. But I hated this movie.
I don't know that I have it in me to tell you just how wrong you are. I don't think I have the mental capacity here.
Well, you're a Tim Burton fan, right?
Apparently not.
Are you a Tim Burton fan, Anthony, in general?

Tim Burton is very hit or miss for me. I find in his later years especially, he's just kind of been repetitive. But I'm not not a fan. I like a lot of his stuff, especially the earlier stuff that came around the time of Edward Scissorhands.

Well, the reason I ask is because Marty does not really like Tim Burton. It doesn't connect with him. He doesn't really enjoy it. So he's never been an Edward Scissorhands fan, but he doesn't really like any Tim Burton stuff. So it surprises me that you don't like Edward Scissorhands, though.
So I do have a few theories as to why, which we'll get into when we get into the episode.
Interesting.
Thom, because you do like this, is that anywhere on the list?
You're so funny, Thom. I will say, I was in a mood last week. I'm a little more mellow now. I had watched it, like, finished it a few minutes before hopping on, and I was ready to rumble.
So you're getting mellow Anthony tonight.
That's probably a good thing. We had some space.

Yes, that's good. See, everything happens for a reason. This movie is an iconic movie for my teenage years, all of my formative years. I was a fan. I watched it quite often. I really enjoy it. It's pretty quintessential Tim Burton. I don't know that there are many movies that get much more Tim Burton-y than this one. And yeah, I like it.
Tim Burton-y. That's accurate.
Is that an adjective that you like?
Oh yeah, it fits. It absolutely suits him.
I like that "Tim Burton-y" can be a compliment and an insult.
No, not really.
Depending on the movie you're referring to, or the years you're referring to.
Disrespectfully agree to disagree.
I mean, there have been some misses for me, but not many. Disrespectfully. Not many at all for me. All right. So let's go through.

Let's run through the credits of this one, y'all. It is, as we said, Tim Burton. We're not going to dwell too long on Tim Burton because we did spend quite a bit of time talking Tim Burton on last year's episode. If you'd like to hear more thoughts on Tim Burton, please go back and check out our Nightmare Before Christmas episode. The music is, of course, for anybody who watched two minutes of this movie will know it is Danny Elfman.
And I feel like we've talked Danny Elfman so much that we're going to go past this as well. the movie stars Johnny Depp as Edward Scissorhands
I don't even know where to begin with Johnny Depp. What's your earliest Johnny Depp memory?
21 Jump Street.
He's so pretty. What's yours, Anthony?
Nightmare on Elm Street.
So you saw that before you saw 21 Jump Street?
Well, yeah, because he's a horror movie fan.
Yeah. But it was still like 1984. That was long before Anthony's time.
Well, I could reasonably see Anthony picking up a horror film.
I guess 21 Jump Street was over long before he would have seen the TV show.
Yeah, it's harder to get into old shows.

Well, it doesn't go any earlier than A Nightmare on Elm Street, because that was Johnny Depp's first foot into film. He was in A Nightmare on Elm Street. He was in Platoon. He had a recurring role on 21 Jump Street. Of course, like we said, he's got Edward Scissorhands. He was in Freddy's Dead: The Final Nightmare.

He was in Benny and June, which is pretty amazing. What's Eating Gilbert Grape, Ed Wood Don Juan DeMarco Donnie Brasco Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas I don't know if you know this or not but he actually had an appearance on The Vicar of Dibley
Yeah, he was in their comic relief special in 1999.
Oh my goodness.
That sentence together is so confusing. I don't know what to do with that.

The Astronaut's Wife. He was in the Sleepy Hollow movie. Chocolat. Blow, a really dark and twisted movie. From Hell. Pirates of the Caribbean. Once Upon a Time in Mexico. Actually, he's in the whole Pirates of the Caribbean franchise. Finding Neverland. The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus. Public Enemies. Alice in Wonderland. Dark Shadows. The Lone Ranger. Mortdecai. Black Mass. Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them; of course, he plays Grindelwald in Harry Potter now, so we've got that reference out of the way. He's just got this long, awesome career. What's your favorite Johnny Depp, guys?
Finding Neverland.
Mine is, oh God, I had it, and I forgot it. That's the right answer.
Oh, I love Benny & Joon.
Oh, it's Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas. It's respectable. Or A Nightmare on Elm Street, or Sleepy Hollow.
Not a big Johnny Depp fan.
Sleepy Hollow bores me so badly I can't get through it. Really?
His developing love interest, Kim, is played by Winona Ryder.
The earliest Winona Ryder I knew of was Beetlejuice, but she had a couple of parts before that. She was in Heathers, Edward Scissorhands of course, Mermaids,

Great Balls of Fire. Bram Stoker's Dracula. The Age of Innocence. Reality Bites. She was Jo in Little Women. How to Make an American Quilt. The Crucible. She was in Alien: Resurrection. Autumn in New York. Girl, Interrupted, which was one of Christine's favorite movies for a long time. Mr. Deeds. She was in Zoolander. She did play a part in one episode of Friends.
Yeah, she did.

She was in Star Trek. She was in Black Swan. She did some other Tim Burton; she was in Frankenweenie. I liked her a lot in Drunk History. And she's probably more known by our younger audience for her role as Joyce Byers in Stranger Things than just about anything else, because she's kind of everywhere right now. Favorite Winona anything, anybody?
I really liked Reality Bites.
Reality Bites.
Mine was Heathers, or Beetlejuice. I really like her in Stranger Things.
I think you and I, Julia, were probably the tail end of the people who really got Reality Bites.
You know what I mean? That was an iconic movie for us. It was perfectly timed for our age. It was.
Peg is played by Dianne Wiest.
You will probably know her from a lot of stuff because she's been acting for quite some time. She was in Independence Day.
She was?
The old one, not the new one. The 1983 version.

She was in The Lost Boys, which is an awesome movie. Little Man Tate. Bullets Over Broadway. The Birdcage. The Horse Whisperer. Practical Magic. She was in that TV miniseries The 10th Kingdom. She did a bunch of Law & Order-type stuff. She was in I Am Sam.
Oh, she's in Dan in Real Life.
She's in Dan in Real Life. I love that movie.
So she was in The Odd Life of Timothy Green, which was also an underrated, awesome movie.
Is that the one with Jennifer Garner?
Yes.
Where they get a kid who's a plant?
Yeah.
I never saw that movie. Is it really good?
It's so good.
Is it a family-movie-night movie?
Absolutely.
Am I going to cry the entire time?
I doubt it. It's just good.
Really? I don't know, it looks like a cry movie.
I didn't cry.
Well, that doesn't mean anything. I cry at everything.

All right. Then we have Jim, who is played by Anthony Michael Hall. Again, an illustrious career, starting with some ABC Weekend Specials. He was in National Lampoon's Vacation. He was in The Breakfast Club. Weird Science. He was on Saturday Night Live.
He did a stint on Tales from the Crypt. And Six Degrees of Separation.
Oh, that's epic.

He was on Murder, She Wrote. Touched by an Angel. More recently, he was in The Dark Knight. More recently being ten years ago now. He was also in Freddy Got Fingered, Hitch, All About the Benjamins, LA Blue. He was on Community and Last Man Standing. And like you said, he's in a new upcoming Halloween movie called Halloween Kills that's filming right now, for 2020. It's a sequel to Halloween, with Jamie Lee Curtis.
Oh, it is? That seems like a bad title.
I know. That's a bad title.
I think the next one, the one after that, is called Halloween Ends. They're shooting them back to back.
Oh man, they're banging out a bunch of new ones, huh?
And there's a lot more cast, but we're gonna stop with Kathy Baker who plays Joyce. She was on the TV show Picket Fences when I was growing up. That's where I knew her from.
In the moment I saw her face, I was reminded of that show.
Bit of a departure. A little bit. Just a little bit.
She was pretty disturbing here. She did a made-for-TV movie about the Oklahoma City bombing.
She was in House Rules. She was in The Glass House. Lots of stuff I've never heard of, y'all. 13 Going on 30.
Oh, I love that movie. That movie is amazing.
It's so good.
It was a great movie. Again, Jennifer Garner. I love her.
She's done a lot of one-off appearances on TV shows.
Julia, do you want to give us a plot synopsis of this movie?
Oh, sorry, I want to mention one other person. Alan Arkin. No, two more people, then.
Okay.
Conchata Ferrell, who plays Helen in this. I want to mention her because, if you remember, we covered her. She was in Krampus as well.
She was in Krampus.
Yeah. So I want to mention her, and then Alan Arkin, because who doesn't want a good opportunity to talk about Alan Arkin?
And we just covered him in Love the Coopers.
We did, so we don't really need to go through anything of his, except for his awesome Sesame Street episodes.
Okay. Now, he has awesome Sesame Street episodes?
He had a character for a season in the '70s.
I didn't know that. Really?
A whole not. We had like five or six episodes in one season. Oh my gosh.
Love him.
Plot synopsis.

In a castle high on top of a hill lives an inventor's greatest creation, Edward, a near complete person. The creator died before he could finish Edward's hands. Instead, he's left with metal scissors for hands. Since then, he's lived alone. until a kind lady named Peg discovers him and welcomes him into her home. At first, everyone welcomes him into the community, but soon things begin to take a change for the worse.
We probably should have mentioned Vincent Price was the inventor as well.
Because he's pretty darn amazing. Except as an inventor.
He wasn't done. He did a pretty darn good job. He did a pretty darn good job of building a near human being.
I don't understand why an unfinished human being would have scissors for him.
Well, you know what, Anthony, if you can't figure that out, I'm not going to tell you. Because he takes him from this utilitarian thing and he turns him into flesh and bone.
It's the dichotomy of Edward Scissorhands.

It's a tragedy, Anthony. It's a tragic story. It's all the love. This movie is a tragedy. And again, I am fully aware I'm the unpopular opinion. I asked just about everyone who passed me at work the day after I watched this movie if they liked this film. I couldn't find anyone who agreed with me. So I'm aware. Sarah loves this film. So I'm aware people are fond of this movie.
Maybe if I had seen it earlier, I would have been fond of it. But for me… I mean, how many years later is it now? Almost 30, right?
Just about. Almost 30. Two years from the 30th anniversary.

How many movies have Tim Burton and Johnny Depp done since this? I know this was their first one, but for me, it was just same old, same old for them. Maybe if I had seen it earlier, before a lot of their later stuff, I would have appreciated it more.
You can't compare this to, say, Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, which was awful.
An abomination.
Absolutely awful, Tim. This is so much better. I mean, you have to feel sorry for him when Kim's like, "Oh, hold me, Edward," or whatever, and he's like, "I can't." That's sad.
I rolled my eyes at that part. So dramatic.
You have no soul.
Because somebody invented me and forgot to put the soul in me.

So, okay. One of my favorite Disney movies is Beauty and the Beast, right? And this is a Beauty and the Beast. This is a Frankenstein-type story. Both films I love, by the way. But there's a great documentary on the making of Beauty and the Beast, the animated one, and they talk about how it took them nearly a year to design the Beast, because it was such a fine line. They couldn't make him too cute, otherwise he's not this horrible, scary beast, and they couldn't make him too scary.

Otherwise, they didn't think Belle would be able to look past it. And they finally settled on what they did after like a year. I don't think they struck a good balance in this one. I'm sorry. Frankenstein's monster, they did. The beast, they did. This guy was terrifying. And I don't buy that this lovely lady, who was my favorite character in the movie, would go into this abandoned, decrepit castle that's clearly abandoned, saying, I'm the evil lady. I'm not here to hurt you. And then Edward comes out of the shadow, snapping his fingers like lobster claws, and she won't go running for the hills. She'd take him home to her family.
That's because she's such a good person. I don't know. Have you never met a multi-level marketing hun before, Anthony? Who would like anything for a sale?

I have Thom. Christine got some, somebody sent her a voicemail on, on Facebook messenger that looked urgent. And it was all about like, oh, hey, Ellie looks so amazing. Blah, blah, blah. By the way, I'm now selling this awesome hair product.
Well, that's like all the emails we get for our website. That's like, help us promote your website.
That's all this lady is. And you know what? She was my favorite character in this film. I thought she was funny and sweet.

She is one of the few sweet characters in this film. That's for sure. So I really think the age at which you are when you watch this probably does have a lot to do with how much you love it. What do we think of the music, Anthony? The music is fantastic.
That is one of my positives for this movie. It's Danny Elfman's favorite soundtrack composition.
Is it really? That's neat.

You could hear the hints in the music, and see in Burton's style what would come a few years later in Batman Returns and The Nightmare Before Christmas. There are definitely early elements of both those films in this one, for sure.
So you think it depends on the age you see it, Julia?

I think it definitely helps. I mean, think about when it came out, in the '90s. I always felt like Johnny Depp looked the way he did, and everybody else looked the way they did, because of trends during the time, right? That grunge era was leaving or coming, I don't know the timing of that. The black, the alienation.
Right. Like Reality Bites, for what it's worth.

Right. That kind of dark look, and the way that they paired it up against that garish, colorful, freakish-haircut world. And these people, they look superficial, they act superficial. They are what they look like. I don't know. What I love most about this movie is the fact that it's about somebody who feels alone and alienated and is accepted by somebody else. It's just such a beautiful love story to me. It gives me all the heart feels.
I agree. And he suffers like he does, and you can feel it when he's laughed at by people and all of that. Johnny Depp does a really good job of expressing that.
You know who was almost cast for this role?
Who?
Tom Cruise. And Macaulay Culkin was considered for the role of Kevin Boggs in this, but he was already doing Home Alone, so he wasn't able to.
Macaulay Culkin. Macaulay Culkin, who will not respond to any of my emails or tweets. Dang it.

So I do want to respond to something you said, Julia, about the age at which you see it. I totally see that point. At the same time, I work with a lot of people older than you two, who would have been past that grunge phase in the '90s when they saw it, and they loved this film.

Well, maybe I didn't express that right. I don't think it was the grunge phase that locked in whether people connected with this or not. I think it's the age I saw it at, when you feel alienated constantly as a teenager. To watch a story of this alienated guy who finds love and finds connection was hopeful. It was a hopeful movie to me. And I feel like when you see it young like that, whether young means a teenager or a preteen, or in your twenties or early thirties, who knows, you can connect with that. Anybody who's had an experience like that, that alienated feeling, can connect with it.
I didn't.
Well, sorry. You're so popular. Everybody loves you.

No, I had a very rough time as a kid, in terms of alienation and getting bullied. And again, this theme has been done in a million movies and books and everything, and this one just didn't do it for me. And when I read that this is Tim Burton's most personal, autobiographical film, I rolled my eyes. I did. I can understand it. I would be fine with it if he didn't have the tagline for this film, the "most gentle man on earth." When I read that, I just thought he was pompous. Okay, so I like how beautiful this film is. It looks like a fairy tale, which it is, so I thought it looked great.

Well, it's supposed to look like a fairy tale, because the movie's filmed through Edward's eyes, right? So when he sees the city that he's never been exposed to, everything is fantastic. Everything is amazing. It's all these new, fresh eyes, and that's how we're supposed to see it.

And again, not to keep comparing it to other films of this nature, but I didn't buy how quickly everyone accepted him. When you look again at these quote-unquote monster films, like Frankenstein or Beauty and the Beast, everyone's terrified of them at first. These people just welcome this guy with lethal knives for hands into their home and neighborhood without any qualms. I don't know. I get it, it's a fairy tale. It's just not…
I get it. So, something interesting, because Avon's a part of this: I learned last week from a Scottish friend that in Scotland it's an insult to tell somebody that their dad sells Avon.
Really? Avon means the same thing over there?
It's the same thing, but it's an insult to say your dad sells Avon.
Oh, that is funny.
I've been using that a few times since I got back. I'm like, "Dude, your dad sells Avon."
He's committed.
Christine's mom still does. They gave her a free van that she won years ago.
Dude, I know.
Was this a Christmas movie?
I don't think it's a Christmas movie

It's definitely a movie set at Christmas. Part of it's set at Christmas. Alan Arkin rolling out that fake snow on the roof just made me happy. Can I just say, I hope I don't have to do that this year. I hope we have real snow.

I liked Alan Arkin's character. I liked the scene at the restaurant where he's like, "And how do you expect to pay for this barbershop? I guess you're going to take out a loan," putting his foot down. "I'm not paying for it. I already took you in."
Any favorite scenes, y'all?
I have a scene that stands out to me, and always has, forever and ever.
Is it the dog-grooming scene? Because that was pretty rad.

No, it's the barbershop scene, where she climbs on top of him. I remember when I was a kid and I first saw that, that was the first naughty-bit movie scene I remember ever seeing. My parents were rapidly fast-forwarding through it and were kind of scandalized by it. And when it came up this time, while I was watching the movie, I almost couldn't watch it, because I'm like, this feels really wrong to watch. But it's so not bad by 2019 standards, right?
It's not at all.
It's just funny, because I felt the shame of however old I was when I first saw it.
Can we talk about that neighbor for a minute?
Hold on, I've got to give Johnny Depp credit in that scene. How did he keep the same expression through everything? I don't know how he did it.
You okay, Anthony? You have to give Johnny Depp credit for building this character with only 169 words. And he still built this character that's so iconic, and everybody knows it.
It's pretty good.
I don't think he's going to give him credit for that, frankly.
It takes a lot to act without words, especially the fewer words you have. I'll give him some credit.

I won't give him credit for his later roles where he keeps playing the same character over and over again. I know, it's like every time I turn on the Pirates of the Caribbean, he's the same guy every time. You're hilarious. Well, let's talk about this neighbor for a minute, okay?
When she first set eyes on him, and she's wondering aloud whether he's nice, or hot, or cold. Like, oh my gosh. How does she fit into the whole Tim Burton autobiographical nature of this?
Yeah, that's a good point.
Who hurt you, Tim? That's what I want to know. Who hurt this guy?

When I picked up my grandma from the airport and told her we were recording this movie tonight, she looked at me like I was crazy. Like, why in the world would a Christmas podcast be recording an episode about Edward Scissorhands?
So how do you feel about the ending? I guess I like the ending, where he kills Jim. Is that his name?
He had it coming.
I remember that always took me by surprise, because he's so gentle.
Yeah, because he's so gentle. So now my next question is, who did you hurt, Tim? Who did you hurt?
That was definitely not where you thought it would go. Like a Beauty and the Beast tale, that's definitely not where this storyline typically goes, right?
That's a definite no. They usually stop themselves from killing him. The Beast is the one who has humanity in that story. So this is definitely a pretty big departure from that.

So, I said earlier I really liked the scenery and everything. I loved the castle, and I loved, in the flashbacks, the machines that created him. Even the gears and everything on them. There are some that look like Jack Skellington's face, total Tim Burton designs.
Oh, for sure. The Oogie Boogie in the mansion.
Yep. You saw the statue of the Oogie Boogie.
One thing I will say, and we'll have to knock this movie down for it, and I feel bad saying it: Winona Ryder's awful in it.
She's young, for sure.
How old was she in this movie? I know how old she was supposed to be. What year was she born?
I don't know, let's look. Winona Ryder, 19.
Blonde hair suited her. I thought she was very pretty in this movie.

She's pretty. I feel like her friends in this film are much more what I would be like in this situation. They're supposed to just sit down around this dinner table, accepting this guy with scissors for hands, this robot, and he's serving them with his fingers. I'd be freaked out. I wouldn't know how to take that.
It looked like good food, so you would probably just eat it, I'm assuming.

And I'm sorry, I don't know. With this movie, I couldn't connect. I didn't buy the romance. There was no point in it where I was like, this is where she fell in love with him. It seemed very quick and rushed and glossed over. So by the time we got to the end, where it's revealed that the old lady telling the story is Winona Ryder, and she doesn't want to go back up to the castle because she doesn't want him to see her in her old age, she wants him to remember her how she was, I didn't feel for her. I was like, okay.
Kind of like Winona Ryder and Johnny Depp in real life and their real relationship. You just felt rushed. Didn't seem authentic.
You didn't feel sorry for them when they broke up.
I guess it's a fairy tale, but you know what? I'm taking on Thom's role of nitpicker tonight. I guess it's a fairy tale. It's magical or whatever, but The snow. The snow when he's cutting the ice.

I love that. I like it. I like the idea, but the way it covers that whole freaking town in snow. Come on. Oh my God. See, you say you get that it's a fairy tale, but you're not acting like you get that it's a fairy tale. You know, when I saw this movie, when I saw the Beauty and the Beast, there's no real human beast out there. This just doesn't make sense. It's ridiculous.
Yes, that's true. It's just ridiculous. You were able to look past that, correct?
Just like I was able to look past how he was carving, and I'm like, wow, this is really magical, the way he's bringing this whole town together.
You weren't able to look past a dog named Olive wishing she was a reindeer, Thom.
There are some things we can't look past. But that was stupid.
And that's how I feel about this man with scissors for hands. I don't understand. He's unfinished. Shouldn't there just have been gloves, or nubs, or stubs at the end? Why did he have scissors?

There was probably a utilitarian purpose that the inventor was using the knives for, and then he died. I don't know. Maybe he was having him trim the shrubbery. He obviously seems to have experience with the topiary and the dog grooming.
The dog grooming was awesome.
I didn't like any of it. I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I didn't like any of it. Julia, am I usually this obnoxious when I don't like something?
Sometimes.
Oh God, I'm sorry, y'all.
You be you.
I just feel bad knowing I could come across as insufferable as Anthony does right now.
You know what? Thom and I were so nice at the beginning, saying how much I missed talking to you guys last week.
I missed you too, before you started making a bunch of dumb comments about a good movie.
I will say, my favorite thing to come out of this movie was that there was an episode of Seinfeld based on this film, that I appreciated.
For real? What Seinfeld episode was about this?
Something with his barber, and Edward Scissorhands played a big part. And now that episode has gone down in my opinion because of this movie.
No, it has not. I'm not a big Seinfeld fan.
There are inequalities in this film.
There are. Seinfeld insists upon itself.
That's how I felt about this film and Tim Burton.
